title: Sowing parsnips
subtitle: Getting parsnip seeds to germinate reliably in a cold spring seedbed
excerpt: Parsnips are sown in February or March direct into the ground. The seed is slow to germinate and short-lived; fresh seed sown in cold soil is more reliable than old seed sown in warm conditions.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section on parsnips. RHS parsnip growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Gertrude Jekyll, Home and Garden (1900), Project Gutenberg. USDA cooperative extension notes on parsnip germination, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fungal disease (Itersonilia pastinacae and related species) that causes brown or orange rot at the shoulder of the root, particularly in wet conditions. Resistant varieties and good drainage reduce incidence. Damaged roots are still edible if the cankered area is cut away.

Sowing two or three seeds at each planting position rather than in a continuous drill. The strongest seedling at each station is kept and the others removed. This wastes some seed but avoids the laborious thinning of a continuous row and makes spacing precise.

content.text: Parsnips go in during February to April in the UK for roots ready to harvest from October onwards. The seed is famously slow and erratic to germinate; using fresh seed from the current year and sowing into a moist, fine seedbed gives the best result. Roots left in the ground over winter improve in flavour after the first hard frost.

February is the earliest date if the soil is workable. Parsnip seed germinates best at 10 to 15°C: cold soil slows germination but doesn't prevent it; warm summer soil (above 20°C) inhibits it. March is the most reliable month for most of the UK. April is the latest sensible sowing; later than that and the growing season is too short for sizeable roots.

Deep, stone-free soil in full sun. Remove all stones to at least 30 cm depth; stones fork the roots and produce distorted shapes. Parsnips do not need a heavily manured bed; a bed used for a previous crop with some residual fertility is fine. Freshly manured soil produces hairy, forked roots. pH 6.5 to 7.5 suits them.

: place two or three seeds 1.5 cm deep at every 15 cm along the row. Rows 30 cm apart. Once the seedlings reach 2 to 3 cm, remove all but the strongest at each station. This avoids disturbing the roots of the ones you keep, which thinning a continuous drill would do.

Parsnip seeds take two to four weeks to germinate in cold spring soil. Many gardeners sow a fast-germinating marker crop (radish, lettuce) in the same row to mark where the parsnips are while they wait. If nothing shows after five weeks, resow with fresh seed; old parsnip seed is notoriously short-lived, losing viability after one year.

Keep the bed weed-free by hoeing between rows from emergence onward. Once plants are 20 cm tall, parsnips compete well with weeds. Water sparingly; parsnips on a heavy soil rarely need irrigation. On sandy soil, a weekly water in dry spells prevents the roots splitting. Leave roots in the ground until required; they store perfectly well in the soil through December, January, and February. attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The issues that come up most often with parsnips.

items.cause: Old seed, dry surface, or soil too warm (late sowing).
items.fix: Always use seed from the current year. Keep the seedbed moist during the two to four week wait. Sow in March rather than May if possible.

items.cause: Stones in the soil, fresh manure, or irregular watering.
items.fix: Remove all stones before sowing. Never apply fresh manure to the parsnip bed. On sandy soil, water consistently through summer to prevent splitting.

items.symptom: Brown or orange rot at the top of the root

items.cause: Fungal infection favoured by wet seasons and soil splash.
items.fix: Grow resistant varieties such as Gladiator, Javelin, or White Gem. Improve drainage. Some canker on the shoulder is normal in wet years; cut it away before cooking.
